ion.title: Ions
ion.cationRule: Positive ion: the atom loses {count, plural, one {# electron} other {# electrons}}, taken from the outermost shell (highest n) first. That is why transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d, even though 4s fills first.
ion.anionRule: Negative ion: the atom gains {count, plural, one {# electron} other {# electrons}}, which go into the next empty subshell in filling order.

molar.title: Molar mass
molar.intro: Type a formula to get its molar mass and mass percentages, and convert between grams, moles, particles and gas volume.
molar.help: Type it plainly: H2SO4, Ca(OH)2, CuSO4.5H2O, SO4^2-. No need for subscripts.
molar.ionNote: For ions, the mass of the electrons gained or lost is ignored (it is tiny).
molar.converterNote: n = m / M · N = n × 6.022 × 10²³ · V = n × {vm} L (gases only).

balance.title: Balance equations
balance.intro: Type an unbalanced equation; the answer comes with an electron-balance solution (for redox reactions) and an algebraic one, plus limiting and excess reagents.
balance.help: Separate substances with “ + ”, join the sides with “->”, “→” or “=”. Write ions as Fe3+, SO4^2- and electrons as e-. Coefficients you type are checked.
balance.givenWrong: Your coefficients aren’t right: see the answer above.
balance.noElectron: No electron-balance solution (not a redox reaction, or an oxidation number couldn’t be assigned with certainty). See the algebraic method.
balance.electronTotal: Electrons transferred in the balanced equation: {count}.
balance.electronNote: Multiply so the electrons lost equal the electrons gained, put the factors into the equation, then balance the remaining elements. Fractional oxidation numbers (like +8/3 in Fe3O4) are averages.

matrix.step1: Each coefficient is an unknown. Each element (and the charge) gives one conservation equation: left total minus right total equals 0.
matrix.step2: Row-reduce the matrix to reduced row echelon form (rank {rank}).
matrix.step3: Set the free unknown to 1 and solve for the rest:

activity.title: Metal activity series
activity.intro: Metals further left are more reactive than metals to their right. Pick a metal to see what it reacts with.
activity.label: Reactivity series of metals
activity.waterYes: Yes, at room temperature: forms a soluble base and releases H₂ gas.
activity.acidYes: Yes: it is before H, so it displaces hydrogen and releases H₂.
activity.acidNo: No: it is after H, so it can’t displace hydrogen.
activity.saltWater: It reacts with the water first (forming a base), so it doesn’t simply displace other metals from their salt solutions.
activity.saltYes: Displaces the metals after it from their salt solutions: {metals}.
activity.saltNone: Can’t displace any metal in the series.
activity.note: Applies to the common school reactions. Nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid are strong oxidizers and behave differently (they even dissolve Cu and Ag).

sim.title: Decay simulation
sim.chartLabel: Chart of the percentage of nuclei left against the number of half-lives elapsed. The dashed line is theory: 100% times (1/2) to the power of the number of half-lives.
sim.hint: Each nucleus decays at a random moment, and nobody can predict which one goes first. But with many nuclei, half of those left decay in every half-life. Press “Re-roll” to see each run deviate slightly from the theoretical line.

notes.n6_14: Carbon-14 is formed continuously in the upper atmosphere when cosmic rays hit nitrogen. Living things take it in along with ordinary carbon, so the ¹⁴C share in their bodies matches the atmosphere. After death no more ¹⁴C is added and it decays away, half-life by half-life. Measuring what is left dates bones, wood or cloth up to about 50,000 years old. IAEA lists the half-life as 5,700 years; many textbooks use 5,730.
notes.n92_238: Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.47 billion years, close to the age of the Earth (about 4.5 billion years). So nearly half of the ²³⁸U present when the Earth formed is still here. It decays through a long chain of daughters and ends at stable lead-206.
notes.n19_40: Potassium-40 makes up about 0.012% of natural potassium and dates from the Earth's formation. It is in potassium-rich food such as bananas and in your own body: thousands of ⁴⁰K nuclei in you decay every second. Most decay by β⁻ to calcium-40; a small share capture an electron to become argon-40 (the basis of K–Ar dating).
notes.n53_131: The thyroid absorbs iodine-131 like ordinary iodine, so it is used to treat an overactive thyroid and thyroid cancer. Its half-life is about 8 days: long enough to work, short enough to fade quickly. It is also one of the radioactive substances released in nuclear accidents.
notes.n27_60: Cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays as it decays and is used in cancer radiotherapy, sterilising medical equipment and irradiating food to preserve it. Its half-life is about 5.3 years, so sources must be replaced regularly.
notes.n55_137: Caesium-137 is a fission product of uranium, so it is found in fallout after nuclear accidents. Its half-life is about 30 years, long enough to contaminate soil for decades.
